lines: OPay priced its New York I.P.O. Then it walked away.
Here is what happened, and what it says about who captures Nigeria's fintech wealth.
In late October, OPay priced sixteen million American depositary shares at nineteen dollars each.
That was the bottom of its range. It meant about three hundred and four million dollars, at a valuation near four billion.
Then, before a single share traded, the deal was called off.
OPay blamed a regulatory inquiry in a foreign jurisdiction.
It did not name the regulator or the subject, and called that market immaterial to its core business.
Anything beyond that is speculation.
Remember: pricing is not closing. No shares settled, so the money was never raised.
Standard Bank had agreed to buy up to two hundred million dollars of shares in a private placement. That depended on the I.P.O.
It is now in limbo, along with a planned secondary listing in Lagos.
The filing shows a fast-growing, profitable business.
Revenue in the first half of 2026 was four hundred and sixty-seven million dollars, up from one hundred and ninety-seven million a year earlier.
Nearly ninety percent of it came from Nigeria.
But the real story is credit.
Loan financing made up just over half of revenue. Payments brought in about twenty-eight percent.
Provisions for credit losses tripled, to one hundred and eighteen million dollars. That is about half of lending revenue.
So investors will price OPay partly as a lender, not just as a payments company.
Now the bigger question. Nigerians generate most of OPay's revenue.
Yet the company is incorporated in the Cayman Islands, headquartered in Singapore, and chose New York.
Venture funds must return dollars. New York offers deep growth capital and liquidity in dollars.
Lagos offers naira, thinner liquidity, and investors who favour dividends.
The briefing argues the fix is plumbing, not mandates.
A growth board on the Nigerian Exchange. A fungible dual-listing corridor. A small late-stage allocation from pension funds.
And a pre-I.P.O. sandbox that surfaces regulatory inquiries before pricing, not after.
What to watch next: who the regulator is, whether OPay refiles, whether Standard Bank's placement survives, and how credit losses move in the second half.
This is analysis, not investment advice.
